The Best French Films of the 2026 New York Film Festival, Ranked

  • By Andrea Meyer
  • October 20, 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 20:28
Instaread

Every fall, as the temperature drops and the leaves go orange and golden, the New York Film Festival offers eager American crowds the best of world cinema. The 64th edition introduced New Yorkers to the buzziest and most beloved films from Cannes, Berlin, Venice, and beyond, plus selected world premieres. Audiences lapped up Cannes Palme d’or winner Fjord and Best Director winner Fatherland; brilliant Venice Grand Jury Prize recipient, Possible Love; and deservingly gushed-about Cannes favorite Club Kid. 

From September 25-October 12, New Yorkers had the honor of seeing new movies by many of the world’s great filmmakers before their official theatrical release: the world premiere of Tony Gilroy’s Behemoth!, starring Pedro Pascal; Mike Leigh’s Tender Loving Care; Ava DuVernay’s 14th; Pedro Almodóvar’s Bitter Christmas; Luca Guadagnino’s Artificial, starring Andrew Garfield as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman; Werner Herzog’s delightfully wacky Bucking Fasterd; Jesse Eisenberg’s The Debut, already getting Oscar buzz for knockout performances by Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti; Chris Rock’s surprising Misty Green; and NAZA, from Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the directors of Oscar-winning documentary No Other Land, which received global attention for its interviews with the men and women carrying out Israel’s systematic bombing of Gaza and killing of Palestinian civilians. Then there was last-minute addition You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes doc, currently killing at the box office and being crowned by many as the movie of the year.

On the French front, including shorts, revivals and French co-productions, there were a total of 25 French films in the lineup this year. Focusing only on French language features, voilà our list of the 12 best, many of which will soon be on the big screen or a streaming service near you.

12. Diary of a Chambermaid

Romanian director Radu Jude’s (Kontinental ’25) first French-language film was inspired by Octave Mirbeau’s 19th century novel, which has previously been adapted by Jean Renoir, Luis Buñuel, and Benoît Jacquot. Sassy Romanian immigrant Gianina (Ana Dumitrașcu) works as a housekeeper and nanny for a bourgeois couple in Bordeaux (Vincent Macaigne and Mélanie Thierry), who take great pride in their liberal tolerance, compassion, and great taste. While caring for their son (Louen Bouteiller), Gianina sends money home to her own young daughter (Sofia Gragoman). In her spare time, she takes a role in a bawdy student production of Diary of a Chambermaid. Early scenes of Gianina rolling her eyes, telling the tone-deaf family to “fuck off” when they’re out of earshot, and indulging their constant demands are darkly funny. The skewering of the family’s hypocrisy and self-involvement also works. But the ludicrously vulgar play and increasingly unreasonable exploitation of Gianina escalate the film to a level of melodrama and ridiculousness that undermines the satire, testing the viewer’s patience and suspension of disbelief.

A release date for Diary of a Chambermaid has not yet been announced. 

11. The Unknown

In a body swap drama directed by Arthur Harari, the Oscar-winning co-screenwriter of Anatomy of a Fall, Parisian photographer David (Niels Schneider) hooks up with a mysterious hottie (Léa Seydoux) at a party and stumbles home to find he is inhabiting her body. He sets out to find her, only to discover that his body is no longer inhabited by Léa Seydoux, but by another woman he had sex with at another party. Freakiest Friday this is not. Closer to Invasion of the Body Snatchers, but more confounding and a lot less fun. The amateur sleuths wonder if a non-human entity might be responsible, but why? Could it be seeking a body—or prey? Maybe it wants to procreate—or simply drive pretty Parisians insane. The film has been polarizing audiences since Cannes, with some viewers embracing the existential body horror, while others squirm, finding the film slow, pretentious, and impenetrable. If it’s an exploration of gender or trans identity, suggested by the discomfort with which the characters regard the bodies in which they are trapped, or a commentary on sexual consent, these ideas are not sufficiently fleshed out. Instead, we get many questions and few answers. Perhaps it’s a meditation on the impossibility of truly knowing a person. In any case, despite strong performances and some poignant scenes, The Unknown feels like a fascinating premise that fizzled. 

Neon acquired The Unknown for distribution and has not announced a release date. 

10. At Night

Experimental British director Beatrice Gibson’s film begins with an epigraph by the late poet Alice Notley: “I am a tone of voice. Warming, shifting, pausing, changing, including, asserting, exulting, including, including, turning & including.”Over the course of one night in Paris, several women, including the filmmaker, ride trains and wander the city, visiting bars and restaurants, making phone calls to friends, lovers, collaborators. In one scene, they gather for a rich, at times charged conversation about being a woman today—a wife, lover, mother, creator. Sometimes they find common ground, and sometimes it’s clear you can’t generalize. The meditative piece, which screened in the experimental Currents section of NYFF, lulls and challenges us, achieving a sense of unease and poetry, launching into a nighttime dreamscape that shapeshifts with unexpected bursts of performance and emotion. The faces onscreen become familiar, but we struggle to lock down precise relationships between them. Race is a recurrent theme: Didi, a Black woman, reveals that she worked on a film with Gibson and was also her nanny. Now her livelihood is uncertain, and she has a son with whom she lives in a shelter. Questions are posed that cannot be answered in the film’s 87 minutes. We simply take in the women’s stories, in an after-hours landscape of creative women searching, discovering, doing their best.

A release date has not yet been announced for At Night. 

9. Dao

The sprawling new film from French Senegalese auteur Alain Gomis (Félicité) cuts back and forth between two events in two countries, a big French country wedding and a memorial service in Guinea-Bissau. The film opens in a casting session, with actors and non-actors auditioning to play the film’s central mother and daughter. The scene reminds us beautifully that this is not a straight feature, but a documentary-narrative hybrid. In a playful moment, one potential mom says she refuses to play a submissive wife, unless she can get revenge and kill her husband. We cut to a scene of Gloria (Katy Correa) and her daughter, Nour (D’Johé Kouadio), both standouts in the auditions, arriving at their ancestral village in Guinea-Bissau for a celebration of Gloria’s father’s life two years after his death. Nour has never visited before, and her relatives can’t get enough of her. Long, largely improvised rituals, daily tasks, lengthy discussions, meals and celebrations are intercut with a lively, traditional French wedding, marked by dancing, singalongs, and long-festering family tensions. While much of the footage is fascinating, the film runs over three hours, at least an hour of which could have been cut without disrupting the narrative. As in many straight documentaries, there was no real script. No real narrative arc, either, which leads to audience squirming, irritation—and possibly imagining how wonderful a two-hour version would be. 

Janus Films acquired the North American to Dao and has not announced a theatrical release  date.

8. For the Moon

Éric Baudelaire’s cinema verité style documentary drops us into the National Institute for Blind Youth in Paris, where he distributes video cameras to five students, all of whom are completely blind or severely visually impaired, to capture footage of themselves and their world. In the resulting collaborative doc, we watch the students make art, show off their rooms, read in Braille, play piano, sing. One performs a soulful rendition of Edith Piaf’s “Je ne regrette rien,” while a friend accompanies her on the piano. We see the students walking with outstretched arms to locate walls, doors, each other. One girl says music represents the students’ strength and joy. They also tell their stories about losing their vision, surgeries, helpless parents. But the students themselves seem to have long ago accepted life without eyesight. Without vision, they say, their other senses are heightened. None come off as self-pitying or focused on their disability. They laugh, sing, and tell their stories without sadness. They appear confident and self-assured. Perhaps the cameras empower the kids to boldly share their lives, offering their most outgoing, performative and assured selves, greedily sharing with us the beauty they find in their lives. 

For the Moon does not yet have a U.S. release date. 

7. The Drift (La Dérive)

Paula Delsol’s 1964 Nouvelle Vague film (playing in the Revivals section) is described in the NYFF catalog as “underseen and criminally overlooked.” Pelsol wrote, directed, and financed the film, which charts the adventures of Jacquie (Jacqueline Vandal), a rebellious young woman who leaves her family in Paris to run off with a flaky musician, who swiftly kicks her to the proverbial curb. From there, while looking for a job, this gutsy woman has romantic and sexual encounters with a series of men—rich, poor, kind, dismissive, shady, supportive, smitten, most of whom she uses for money, sex, or a place to sleep. In a 1963 interview, Delsol said she “wanted to show that women were looking to be the equal of men in terms of their sexual freedom, and that in playing that game they would always be beaten.” While some of Delsol’s New Wave cohort—François Truffaut, Jean Rouch—championed the film, it was largely forgotten until a recent 4K restoration by the Cinematheque Française. In its daring openness about female sexuality and Jacquie’s open defiance when it comes to marriage and children, the film saw little financial success and is only now being reassessed as a frank exploration of feminism in the 1960s. The film appears as #25 on the New Yorker film critic Richard Brody’s list of “The Greatest Independent Films of the Twentieth Century.”

The Drift is not currently available in theaters or streaming channels. However, you may be able to watch it here, where the film is available for free, at least for now.

6. Red Rocks

In a stunning seaside town in the south of France, six-year-old Géo (Kaylon Lancel) roams aimlessly with his buddies Manon (Louise Podolski) and Rouben (Mohamed Coly). Mainly they scramble up the red cliffs overlooking the sea and jump into the treacherous water below. It stops your heart—and makes you wonder where the hell their parents are. One day another young trio arrives at their favorite spot: B (Alessandro Piquera), Do (Meryl Pires), and Eve (Kelsie Verdeilles). Géo and Eve lock eyes. The pair starts hanging out, even visiting the dazzling villa where Eve lives with her mother and her grandfather in Italy. There’s very little back story, but the scenes trigger questions of class, of townies vs. those who “summer.” In any case, the baby romance—described in the NYFF program as “a kind of pre-preadolescent Romeo and Juliet, complete with rival gangs and puppy love”—inspires big feelings in B, Eve’s amoureux (if a 6-year-old can have one), and Manon who, faced with a rival, develops romantic feelings for Géo. The film is directed by Bruno Dumont, whose award-winning early social realist work (L’humanité, Flandres) often featured non-professional actors and acts of extreme violence and sexuality. Later, he shifted to absurdist comedies like France and The Empire. Here, the mature Dumont uses documentary-style realism to tell the story of a love triangle that interrupts a kind of idyll, where children run unfettered, without adult supervision or concerns. Even the potential danger of jumping off the towering red rocks exists primarily in the imagination of adult viewers accustomed to worrying about the safety of children.

Red Rocks is scheduled for a 2027 theatrical release.

5. A Man of His Time

When we meet Henri Marre (Swann Arlaud), he is a broke, jobless political strategist, looking for work and peddling his self-published book Notre Salut (Our Salvation) to anyone willing to take a free copy. Directed by Emmanuel Marre, the subject’s great-grandson, and based on a trove of letters exchanged between his great-grandparents, the winner of the Cannes prize for best screenplay uses Marre’s story to explore the Nazi occupation of France. After kissing the requisite fesses—and transporting an official’s beloved cat over the demarcation line at night by bicycle—Marre lands a job in the Ministry of Labor. While he views himself as a deeply patriotic, anti-authoritarian French nationalist and supporter of Maréchal Pétain’s interim government, Marre is also opportunistic, motivated by vanity and financial desperation. He relishes his paltry tasks, convinced he is saving France, only to realize too late that he’s nothing but a cog in the fascist machinery. Most haunting, without quite realizing what is happening around them, petty bureaucrats like Marre become complicit in the German transport of French Jews. As historical fiction, the film is fresh and powerful. Its poetry comes in voiceover from letters to Marre from his wife, Paulette (Sandrine Blancke), who struggling to survive back home, her anger and disappointment raging like electric storm clouds off the page. When she finally joins Marre with their children in an attractive apartment once owned by a Jewish family, we learn just how brilliant and charismatic she is, and how intolerant of her husband’s delusional self-aggrandizement and his foolish ignorance of his true place in history.

Distributor 1-2 Special acquired A Man of His Time for 2027 release. 

4. Iron Boy

Former Pixar animator Louis Clichy (Wall-E, Up) reaches into his own past to tell a coming-of-age story about a boy in a back brace on a farm in the Beauce region of France. Eleven-year-old Christophe (voiced by Clichy’s son, Gary) can’t stand up straight. When posing for picture day, he keeps tilting and ruining the shot. While that provides a funny moment, it’s less amusing when he tilts while taking out the family tractor and crashes. Once the family has sold the sheep Christophe loved to pay for a new tractor, he’s fitted for a metal brace he’s forced to wear 24 hours a day, even in bed. Grumpy and bored on the struggling farm, he finds new skills (shelling beans and turning pages for the church organ player) and passions (like playing the organ, and an older bad girl who teaches him how to shoplift). When he fights with his dad, yowls at the universe, or feels joy, a kiss of magical realism makes the world bend and tilt, setting people floating, farm animals soaring, and tiles flying off the rooftops with his overblown emotions. In the end, the family is forced to overcome its petty disagreements to save the farm. There are no easy solutions, but everyone has learned and grown, especially Christophe, in a lovely tale in watercolor strokes so beautiful, you will catch your breath and dream of the French countryside.

Iron Boy will open in theaters on January 22, 2027.

3. Minotaur

As France’s official entry for the Best International Feature Oscar, we are including Minotaur, even though it is not in French, but Russian. The film is eligible as a French co-production by a celebrated director, Andrey Zvyagintsev (Leviathan, The Return), who has been granted asylum in France. A faithful remake of New Wave director Claude Chabrol’s 1969 noir, La femme infidèle, Minotaur is the story of Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov), the successful CEO of a shipping company who discovers that his wife, Galina (Iris Lebedeva), is having an affair. The domestic conflict and its shocking lurch into violence is gripping. But placing the familiar trope in a corrupt patriarchy, where corporate leaders are ordered by the mayor to give up a specified number of their own employees to be drafted in the early days of the war against Ukraine, elevates the smoldering story of desperation and revenge to something darker and more global in reach. Is Gleb’s or Galina’s the greater betrayal? In a world where the patriarch is blameless, what options exist for an intelligent, beautiful woman suffocating in her gilded cage? The political and personal merge seamlessly, the target authoritarianism—in politics, in the home—and Russia in particular. When Zvyagintsev was awarded the Grand Prix at Cannes, he spoke directly to Putin to say, “Put an end to this slaughter. The whole world is waiting for it.” He was named an enemy of the state and chose to remain in exile. 

Minotaur will premiere in theaters on November 20.

2. All of a Sudden

In another complex, profound story by Japanese director Ryusuke Hamaguchi (Drive My Car), ubiquitous French actress Virginie Efira plays Marie-Lou, the director of a nursing home in a Parisian suburb. Marie-Lou is introducing a new caregiving program she deeply believes in called “Humanitude,” which stresses compassion and recognizing the residents’ dignity. Many of her seasoned staff resist the shift, which requires adherence to the program’s many precise guidelines. Overworked and exhausted, Marie-Lou meets a developmentally disabled boy, Tomoki (Kodai Kurosaki) running alone in a park. She delivers him to his grandfather, Gorô (Kyōzō Nagatsuka) and his friend, Mari (Tao Okamoto), who invites Marie-Lou to an experimental play she is directing, in which Tomoki and Gorô star. After the relevant and dazzling performance, Marie-Lou and Mari spend an evening together, moving easily between French and Japanese as they talk about their life philosophies in a way that connects and inspires them in transcendent, life-changing ways. With Mari, Marie-Lou is able to restructure the care facility in ways she could not alone, considering the staff’s needs, finding hidden stores of compassion in herself. The film attains a transcendent vision that leaves the viewer floating, imagining kinder, more generous interactions between people becoming the norm. An unattainable, even utopian idealism suddenly seems possible. And the beauty of that is a gift. Efira and Okamoto shared the award for Best Actress at Cannes this year. 

All of Sudden will be in theaters on November 25.

1. La Gravida

Marine Atlan’s stunning feature debut opens on a teenage boy, Toni (Colas Quignard), watching another boy and a girl in his class have sex through the window of a train compartment. Another girl, Suzanne (Suzanne Gerin), stands still as a shadow, watching him watching them. A minute later Toni is goofing around, dancing down the aisle, annoying their exasperated Latin teacher (Antonia Buresi) as usual. The trio is part of a group of high school kids on a school trip to Pompeii. The one having sex was James (Mitia Capellier-Audat), the golden boy everyone wants a piece of. He’s also best friends with Toni: the screwup, attention hound, openly queer kid swiping potential hookups on Grindr, bragging about his Neapolitan grandmother whose rich lover, his presumed grandfather, reportedly perished in the 1980 Naples earthquake that destroyed the family estate. In this historical site, where beauty and death battle for preeminence, these young lives are forever changed. Director Atlan is a cinematographer, and her visual virtuosity is on full display (along with co-director of photography Pierre Mazoyer). But it’s the writing and direction that grab you by the throat. It’s no wonder the film won the top prize at Cannes Critics’ Week. Atlan masterfully drops us into this fleeting moment of lives on the cusp of adulthood so easily, so realistically, the chatter so achingly authentic, we forget we’re watching a movie and sink deeply into the gossip, the feels, the passions and insecurities. Feeling the exquisite longing and disillusionment so profoundly can only lead these kids—and the deeply invested audience—to devastation. With this tender, immersive, and tragic masterpiece, Atlan has quite possibly reinvented the coming-of-age story in ways both sublime and brutal. It might be the best film of the year.

La Gradiva will be released in theaters on December 18.

Andrea Meyer has written creative treatments for commercial directors, a sex & the movies column for IFC, and a horror screenplay for MGM. Her first novel, Room for Love (St. Martin’s Press) is a romantic comedy based on an article she wrote for the New York Post, for which she pretended to look for a roommate as a ploy to meet men. A long-time film and entertainment journalist and former indieWIRE editor, Andrea has interviewed more actors and directors than she can remember. Her articles and essays have appeared in such publications as Elle, Glamour, Variety, Time Out NY, and the Boston Globe.
